config.title: Build client side pagination for a list

intro.title: Build client side pagination for a list
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a client-side pagination system for a list of items using plain JavaScript. You will learn how to split a large dataset into smaller, manageable pages that users can navigate through. The core programming concepts involved are array manipulation and state management to track the current page. You will use JavaScript functions, event listeners, and DOM manipulation to create interactive 'Previous' and 'Next' buttons. By the end, you will have a functional paginated list that updates dynamically without reloading the page.
intro.usecase: Client-side pagination is essential for managing large datasets in web applications without overwhelming users or servers. You'll see this pattern in e-commerce product listings, where thousands of items are divided into manageable pages for browsing. It's also crucial in admin dashboards displaying user data, analytics tables, and content management systems where editors navigate through articles or media libraries. As a developer, implementing this improves user experience by reducing initial load times and allowing smooth navigation through content sections.

objectives: Implement a state variable to track the current page number
Configure a function to calculate the start and end indices for paginated data
Apply slicing logic to display only the current page's items from the full dataset
Construct interactive buttons to navigate between pages
Initialize and update the UI to reflect the current page and total pages
Bind event handlers to navigation controls for changing pages
Render pagination controls that dynamically adjust based on the dataset size

steps.title: Import React and useState
steps.instruction: Import React and the useState hook from the 'react' library.
steps.hint: Use the import statement to bring in both React and useState from 'react'.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: importing React and useState
import React, { useState } from 'react';
steps.expectedOutcome: You'll have React and useState available to use in your component.
successCriteria: React and useState are imported from 'react'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're importing both React and useState from 'react'.
steps.feedbackWrong: That's not quite right. You need to import both React and useState from the 'react' library.

steps.title: Create the main Pagination component
steps.instruction: Create a functional component named Pagination that returns an empty div element.
steps.hint: Define a function called Pagination that returns JSX containing a single <div> element.
steps.seedCode:
import React, { useState } from 'react';

// Create the Pagination component here
steps.expectedOutcome: A Pagination component is defined that returns an empty div.
successCriteria: The component is named Pagination and returns a <div> element.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure the component is named exactly 'Pagination' and returns a <div> element.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component isn't defined correctly. Create a function named Pagination that returns a <div>.

steps.title: Initialize the data array
steps.instruction: Inside the Pagination component, create a constant array of 50 items (numbers 1 through 50) that will be paginated.
steps.hint: You can create an array using Array.from() or a simple loop. For example, create an array with numbers from 1 to 50.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: creating an array of items
const items = Array.from({ length: 50 }, (_, i) => i + 1);
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have a data array containing numbers 1 through 50 ready for pagination.
successCriteria: A constant array with 50 items (numbers 1-50) is created inside the Pagination component.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've created an array, but make sure it contains exactly 50 items (numbers 1 through 50).
steps.feedbackWrong: The data array wasn't created correctly. Create a constant array with numbers 1 through 50 inside the component.

steps.title: Initialize state for current page
steps.instruction: Inside the Pagination component, use useState to create a state variable named 'currentPage' and initialize it to 1.
steps.hint: Call useState(1) and destructure the returned array into two variables: currentPage and setCurrentPage.
steps.analogousExample:
// Similar: state for a counter
const [count, setCount] = useState(0);
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have a state variable to track which page is currently displayed.
successCriteria: The useState hook is called with initial value 1, and the destructured variables are named currentPage and setCurrentPage.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure you're calling useState(1) and destructuring the array into [currentPage, setCurrentPage].
steps.feedbackWrong: Try again. You need to use useState to create a state variable for the current page.

steps.title: Initialize state for items per page
steps.instruction: Inside your Pagination component, use the useState hook to create a state variable named 'itemsPerPage' and initialize it to 10.
steps.hint: Add a new useState call after your existing state for current page. The pattern is: const [itemsPerPage, setItemsPerPage] = useState(10);
steps.analogousExample:
// Similar: state for tracking items per page
const [itemsPerPage, setItemsPerPage] = useState(10);
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have a state variable 'itemsPerPage' with an initial value of 10, ready to control how many items display per page.
successCriteria: A state variable named 'itemsPerPage' is declared using useState and initialized to 10.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're using useState to create a variable named 'itemsPerPage' with an initial value of 10.
steps.feedbackWrong: Use the useState hook to create a state variable called 'itemsPerPage' and set it to 10.

steps.title: Calculate pagination indexes
steps.instruction: Inside your Pagination component, calculate the index of the last item for the current page and the index of the first item for the current page based on the currentPage state and itemsPerPage state.
steps.hint: You'll need to use the current page number and items per page to compute these indexes. The last item index is currentPage * itemsPerPage, and the first item index is lastItemIndex - itemsPerPage.
steps.expectedOutcome: Two variables are declared that hold the start and end indexes for slicing the data array to get the current page's items.
successCriteria: The component contains calculations for lastItemIndex and firstItemIndex using currentPage and itemsPerPage.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're calculating both indexes correctly. Remember: lastItemIndex = currentPage * itemsPerPage, and firstItemIndex = lastItemIndex - itemsPerPage.
steps.feedbackWrong: The pagination indexes aren't calculated correctly. You need to compute both lastItemIndex and firstItemIndex based on the current page and items per page.

steps.title: Slice the data for current page
steps.instruction: Inside your component, use the slice() method to extract the items for the current page from the data array and store them in a variable called currentItems.
steps.hint: The slice() method takes two arguments: start index and end index. Use your calculated startIndex and endIndex variables.
steps.expectedOutcome: You should have a variable named currentItems that contains only the items from the data array that belong on the current page.
successCriteria: The currentItems variable is declared using slice() with startIndex and endIndex.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're using slice() with the correct start and end indexes.
steps.feedbackWrong: The slice operation wasn't completed correctly. Remember to use slice(startIndex, endIndex) on the data array.

steps.title: Create handler for next page
steps.instruction: Inside your Pagination component, create a function named handleNextPage that increments the currentPage state by 1.
steps.hint: Remember to use the setCurrentPage function from useState to update the state value.
steps.expectedOutcome: You should have a handleNextPage function that updates the currentPage state when called.
successCriteria: The handleNextPage function is defined and uses setCurrentPage to increment the currentPage value.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've created a function, but make sure it properly increments the currentPage state using setCurrentPage.
steps.feedbackWrong: The handleNextPage function is missing or doesn't properly update the currentPage state.

steps.title: Create handler for previous page
steps.instruction: Create a function named handlePreviousPage that decrements currentPage by 1, ensuring it doesn't go below 1.
steps.hint: Inside your component, define a function that uses setCurrentPage with a condition to check if currentPage is greater than 1 before decreasing it.
steps.expectedOutcome: A handlePreviousPage function is defined that safely decreases the current page number.
successCriteria: The handlePreviousPage function is defined, uses setCurrentPage, and prevents currentPage from going below 1.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your function properly checks that currentPage doesn't go below 1.
steps.feedbackWrong: The function isn't quite right. Remember to create a function named handlePreviousPage that decreases currentPage by 1, but not below 1.

steps.title: Render the current page items
steps.instruction: Inside your component, map over the data array to render each item in a list. Use the startIndex and endIndex to slice the data for the current page.
steps.hint: Use the slice method on the data array with startIndex and endIndex to get the current page items, then map over them to create list elements.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will be able to display the current page's items when the return statement is updated.
successCriteria: The data array is sliced using startIndex and endIndex, and the resulting items are mapped to create list elements.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure to use both startIndex and endIndex with slice, and map over the result.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check that you're using slice with the correct indexes and mapping over the resulting array to create list items.

steps.title: Add previous and next buttons with click handlers
steps.instruction: Add a 'Previous' button that calls the handlePreviousPage function and a 'Next' button that calls the handleNextPage function inside your component's return statement.
steps.hint: Use the <button> element with onClick handlers. Place both buttons after your current page items list.
steps.expectedOutcome: Two interactive buttons ('Previous' and 'Next') appear in the UI that will navigate through pages when clicked.
successCriteria: The component returns a 'Previous' button with onClick={handlePreviousPage} and a 'Next' button with onClick={handleNextPage}.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You added buttons, but check that each button has the correct onClick handler: Previous button should call handlePreviousPage, Next button should call handleNextPage.
steps.feedbackWrong: The buttons are missing or not properly connected to the handler functions. Add both buttons with the correct onClick attributes.

steps.title: Display current page and total pages
steps.instruction: Inside your component's return statement, add a paragraph that shows the current page number and total number of pages. Calculate total pages by dividing data length by itemsPerPage and rounding up.
steps.hint:
Use Math.ceil() to round up the division result. Display it in a

tag with clear text.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will show a paragraph with the current page and total pages when rendered.
successCriteria: A paragraph element displays the current page number and total pages using Math.ceil() for calculation.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure you're calculating total pages correctly with Math.ceil() and displaying both current page and total pages in the paragraph.
steps.feedbackWrong: The pagination status isn't displaying correctly. Check that you're calculating total pages with Math.ceil(data.length / itemsPerPage) and showing both values in a paragraph.
